title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
abstract: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $κ$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.
summary: This work analyzes the thermalization dynamics in 3D classical many-body systems, revealing that the energy distributions transiently deviate from the expected Maxwell-Boltzmann form towards $\kappa$-distributions. Furthermore, it rigorously examines how the scaling of the interaction energy depends on the anisotropy of the trapping potential, linking it to effective dimensionality exponents.
main_problem: The paper investigates the dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems, focusing on deviations from expected Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions and the influence of anisotropic trapping.
main_result: The system exhibits transient non-Maxwellian energy distributions, characterized by $\kappa$-distributions, and the scaling of the interaction energy exponent ($\alpha$) depends critically on the trapping anisotropy and interaction range.
method: The study employs numerical simulations of the equations of motion derived from a complex Hamiltonian, supplemented by analytical derivations of scaling exponents and iterative equations for inverse temperatures.
model_or_system: The model involves two interacting baths of harmonic oscillators in three dimensions, described by a Hamiltonian that includes both free harmonic oscillator terms and an interaction term. The analysis extends from 1D to 3D systems.
key_observables: Energy distribution shape ($\kappa$-distributions vs. MB), peak location ($E_{\max}$), peak probability density ($p_{\max}$), and the anomalous scaling exponent ($\alpha$) of the interaction energy.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($\gamma$), interaction range ($\lambda$), and the degree of trapping anisotropy (frequency ratios $\omega_x : \omega_y : \omega_z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations for the average interaction energy and assumes that scaling behavior can be mapped onto effective dimensionality, though limitations exist for very strong coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of the energy distribution peak on binning choices, the deviation factor $\xi(\kappa)$ over time, and the scaling exponent $\alpha$ as a function of the interaction range $\lambda$ for different trapping geometries.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the non-Maxwellian nature of the energy distribution in 3D, then analyzing the time evolution of this deviation using a dimensionless ratio $\xi(\kappa)$, and finally investigating the scaling of the interaction energy exponent $\alpha$ under varying degrees of trapping anisotropy.
why_interesting: The study provides detailed insights into non-equilibrium dynamics, showing how transient non-Maxwellian states ($\kappa$-distributions) emerge during thermalization, which is crucial for understanding energy transport in complex, interacting quantum/classical systems.
